strengths: A useful dataset for the community of digital humanities, covering a gap of low resources data.
The dataset has been rigorously constructed, with layout annotations.
In addition to the language, the documents in the dataset have some particularities that make it interesting to tackle language-independent document layout analysis and recognition problems.
The complementary pipeline processing that is presented is a good way to illustrate the value of the dataset, comparing the processing with other datasets.
This paper presents a new historical German newspaper dataset, providing layout information and text line annotations, and also offers some baselines for layout detection and OCR tasks.

The paper makes a significant contribution by providing a new, large, and annotated dataset of 693 high-resolution historical newspaper pages in German Fraktur, addressing a crucial gap in resources for processing German-language historical documents.
Chronicling Germany dataset introduces OCR as well as polygon layout analysis problem for historical newspaper scans
Compared to Dell 2024, Chronicling Germany appears to have much more complex layouts. This could introduce a new line of problems in historic document analysis
The paper is well written and easy to follow
weaknesses: Presenting a new dataset requires a solid justification of its usefulness, and the annotated historical newspaper dataset is not in the mainstream of the representation learning community, limiting its relevance to a marginal audience.

It is unclear whether cross‑fold validation was performed; the proposed pipeline was not tested on the American Stories dataset nor was the Dell et al. pipeline tested on the German dataset, and different datasets and methods should be used for comparison.

The novelty and contribution of this paper is limited; the main contribution is the historical German newspaper dataset itself, which does not have significant uniqueness in size and diversity compared to existing datasets [1][2][3].
Lack of quantitative comparison with existing datasets, which fails to show the superiority of the Chronicling Germany dataset.
Lack of detailed assessment of the annotation quality, such as the review of annotation consistency.
Section 5 does not provide detailed results of testing on out‑of‑distribution (OOD) data, which is insufficient to reflect the generalizability of the pipeline.
The paper incorrectly used the ICLR 2024 template instead of the ICLR 2025 one.
The paper does not cite significant existing projects that contributed to newspaper recognition, such as Newseye and Impresso.
While the OCR-D project is mentioned only in the annex, it should be highlighted in the main text.
The study does not leverage high‑performance OCR systems such as Pero‑OCR, which could have enhanced baseline OCR results; this limits the impact of the findings.

The paper’s reliance on an OCR system that requires baseline detection is questionable, as such systems are typically designed for non‑horizontal or curved text, which is rare in newspaper layouts; a retrained OCR model leveraging pre‑existing models on platforms like HuggingFace would likely be more suitable.

The use of a relatively older UNet model for layout detection is debatable, given that more recent and effective models like YOLO‑based architectures outperform UNet; Table 3's comparison highlights these limitations and suggests poor generalization capabilities.

The full evaluation of the pipeline is limited; only a Character Error Rate of 6% is reported without further details, and article separation is not assessed, making the results appear preliminary and potentially incomplete.
The legend for Table 3 lacks clarity, especially regarding what is meant by “F1 Score in distribution”.

The authors claim that modern human readers will struggle reading the contents of Chronicling Germany, but only provide examples of font differences; they should also focus on difficulties for modern readers to understand layout differences.
The authors did not provide information regarding the image sizes or DPI, which could help researchers evaluate the usefulness of the dataset.
The benchmark methods don’t seem well justified; it is unclear whether existing pipelines trained on modern newspaper were explored on this dataset.
There is no information about the legibility of the data.
Given that comprehending the pages is not trivial for modern German readers, it is unclear why reading order is within the scope of this dataset.
How was the reading order automatically assigned and evaluated to have “satisfactory results”?
